triage.name: E. coli Infections
triage.reason: A specific pathogen with distinct clinical syndromes (UTI, gastroenteritis, sepsis) that students diagnose via history, exam and cultures.

age.peak: bimodal: young children and older adults

demographics: Urinary tract infections from E. coli are far more common in women than men
Enteric (diarrheal) E. coli infections affect both sexes and are most common in young children and older adults
Bloodstream infections are more common in hospitalized and older patients

risk_factors.text: Female anatomy (short urethra) for urinary tract infection
Sexual activity or recent new sexual partner for urinary tract infection
Undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized milk or juice, or contaminated produce
Contact with farm animals or petting zoos
Recent antibiotic use or hospitalization (for resistant or healthcare-associated strains)
Urinary catheter or recent urinary instrumentation

social_history: Recent travel, especially to areas with poor sanitation
Attendance at daycare or contact with a child in daycare
Food prepared or eaten at a restaurant or large gathering
exposures: Raw or unwashed vegetables and sprouts
Close contact with a person who has diarrhea

chief_complaints.text: I have bad stomach cramps and diarrhea
I have a fever and feel awful

hpi.onset: Diarrheal illness starts abruptly, often 1–3 days after exposure; urinary symptoms build over 1–2 days
hpi.duration: Diarrhea usually lasts 5–10 days; urinary symptoms progress over hours to days
hpi.progression: Watery diarrhea may become bloody over 1–2 days; urinary symptoms may progress from burning to flank pain and fever
hpi.location: Lower abdomen for enteric infection; suprapubic or flank for urinary infection
hpi.radiation: Flank pain may radiate to the groin or back in pyelonephritis
hpi.quality: Crampy abdominal pain; burning or stinging with urination
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; cramps can be 7–8/10
hpi.timing: Cramps come in waves before bowel movements; urinary burning is constant with voiding
pertinent_negatives: Bloody diarrhea with no prior watery stools

positives.text: Going to the bathroom more often

argues_against: Flank pain with high fever and chills suggests kidney involvement

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants and young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, and fever without localizing symptoms; bloody diarrhea can be the first sign.
May have milder fever and less pain but more risk of dehydration, confusion, and progression to bloodstream infection.
Higher risk of invasive disease, including bloodstream infection and sepsis, with less prominent gastrointestinal symptoms.
Urinary tract infection is more likely to ascend to the kidney and can trigger preterm labor; symptoms may be attributed to normal pregnancy discomfort.

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing, mild discomfort, able to converse and move comfortably
general.moderate: Ill-appearing but interactive, uncomfortable, prefers to lie still during cramps
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, visibly uncomfortable, reluctant to move
general.critical: Lethargic or confused, pale or mottled, diaphoretic, may be obtunded

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting away from the area of maximal pain
findings.finding: Diffuse or lower abdominal tenderness without focal peritoneal signs
Costovertebral angle tenderness on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen gently and then deeply
Ask the patient to cough, or gently release deep pressure
Auscultate the abdomen in all four quadrants
Palpate the right upper quadrant during inspiration
Auscultate the heart and palpate the radial pulse
Perform a pelvic exam when a gynecologic cause is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness or adnexal mass

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and level of consciousness

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not exclude E. coli infection, especially in early gastroenteritis or in older adults.
Falls with heavy bloody diarrhea or hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Thrombocytopenia is a hallmark of hemolytic uremic syndrome after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.
Rising creatinine with anemia and low platelets suggests hemolytic uremic syndrome; also rises with dehydration or pyelonephritis.
Rises with dehydration and poor intake.
Hypokalemia from diarrhea; hyperkalemia can occur with acute kidney injury.
Metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss in diarrhea or from sepsis.
Elevated lactate with hypotension or organ dysfunction suggests sepsis from a bloodstream infection.
Supports a bacterial cause and invasive disease but does not identify the organism.
Present in urinary tract infection; a negative result makes urinary infection much less likely.
Positive nitrite is fairly specific for Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or antibiotics; pregnancy changes management of urinary infection.

findings.finding: Nonspecific ST-T changes with severe sepsis or electrolyte disturbance

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Adults with severe abdominal pain, suspected abscess, or when another cause of acute abdomen must be excluded

findings.text: Colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding
Dilated fluid-filled loops of small and large bowel
No abscess or free air in uncomplicated colitis
Intra-abdominal abscess or free air suggesting perforation

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When IV contrast cannot be given (allergy, kidney injury)

findings.text: Bowel wall thickening and surrounding inflammatory change
Less sensitive for abscess than contrast-enhanced study

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the abdomen (right upper quadrant and kidneys)
imaging.preferred_when: Children and pregnancy; suspected biliary or renal source

findings.text: Hydronephrosis or renal enlargement in pyelonephritis

imaging.preferred_when: Recurrent or complicated urinary infection in adults

findings.text: Normal upper tracts in most uncomplicated infections
Obstructing stone or urinary tract abnormality
Usually nonspecific; may show dilated bowel loops or a radiopaque stone

initial.why: Looks for leukocytosis, anemia, and thrombocytopenia (hemolytic uremic syndrome)
Assesses dehydration, electrolytes, bicarbonate, and kidney function
Screens for urinary tract infection with leukocyte esterase, nitrite, and bacteria
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and guides antibiotic choice
Identifies E. coli and other bacterial causes in bloody or severe diarrhea
Detects bloodstream infection in fever, rigors, or sepsis
initial.only_if: fever, rigors, hypotension, or other signs of sepsis

initial.why: Screens for sepsis and tissue hypoperfusion
initial.only_if: hypotension, tachycardia, or concern for sepsis

confirmatory.why: Confirms E. coli urinary tract infection and guides antibiotic choice

supporting.why: Supports a bacterial cause and tracks response
Supports bacterial infection and invasive disease
Identifies Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and guides avoidance of antibiotics
supporting.only_if: bloody diarrhea or suspected hemolytic uremic syndrome

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Excludes abscess, perforation, or another acute abdomen
supporting.only_if: severe abdominal pain, peritoneal signs, or suspected abscess

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless pain is epigastric or pancreatic disease is suspected
No role in infectious diarrhea or urinary infection
Does not help diagnose an acute infection
Not part of the acute workup
Rarely changes management of uncomplicated infection
Not needed for a first uncomplicated urinary infection

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging or antibiotics in anyone who could be pregnant
Stool culture and Shiga toxin testing before antibiotics in bloody diarrhea, since antibiotics may increase the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
Blood cultures before antibiotics when sepsis is suspected
Urine culture before antibiotics in urinary infection to guide therapy

differential.name: Salmonella infection
differential.why_considered: Both cause acute watery or bloody diarrhea with fever and abdominal cramps after a food exposure.
differential.trigger: Bloody diarrhea with fever after undercooked poultry, eggs, or contact with reptiles.

history: Exposure to undercooked poultry, eggs, or reptiles
Diarrhea may be prolonged or relapsing
exam: Rose spots are rare but suggest enteric fever
labs: Stool culture grows Salmonella, not E. coli
Blood culture may be positive in invasive disease
imaging: Usually normal; may show nonspecific bowel wall thickening

differential.name: Campylobacter infection
differential.why_considered: Leading cause of bacterial bloody diarrhea with cramps and fever.

history: Exposure to undercooked poultry or unpasteurized milk
Diarrhea may be bloody and last longer than E. coli
Can be followed by reactive arthritis
exam: May have rebound tenderness if colitis is severe
imaging: Usually normal; may show colitis on CT

differential.name: Shigella infection
differential.why_considered: Causes bloody diarrhea with fever and cramps, often with small-volume stools.

history: Exposure to contaminated food or water, or close contact with an infected person
imaging: Usually normal; may show colonic thickening

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Common cause of watery diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps.

labs: Stool studies negative for bacterial pathogens
Normal or mildly elevated white count

differential.name: Urinary tract infection (non-E. coli)
differential.why_considered: E. coli is the most common cause, but other bacteria can cause identical urinary symptoms.

labs: Urinalysis with leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and white blood cells
Urine culture grows a different organism

differential.name: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (other causes)
differential.why_considered: Can present with bloody diarrhea followed by anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury, but may be caused by other pathogens or conditions.
differential.trigger: Bloody diarrhea followed by pallor, decreased urine output, and petechiae.

labs: Negative stool culture for E. coli O157:H7 in some cases

severity.mild: Uncomplicated watery diarrhea or cystitis; able to tolerate oral fluids, no fever or low-grade fever, no blood in stool, normal kidney function.
severity.moderate: Persistent diarrhea with dehydration, fever, or dysuria with suprapubic pain; may have leukocytosis but no organ dysfunction.
severity.severe: Bloody diarrhea with severe cramps, fever, dehydration, or pyelonephritis with flank pain and systemic symptoms; may have acute kidney injury or electrolyte abnormalities.
severity.critical: Sepsis with hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status, or hemolytic uremic syndrome with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury requiring dialysis.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests Shiga toxin-producing E. coli or other invasive pathogen; risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome.
May indicate dehydration or acute kidney injury from hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Suggests anemia and thrombocytopenia, possibly hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Suggests severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or sepsis.

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs
red_flags.meaning: Suggests perforation or another acute abdomen.

complications.name: Hemolytic uremic syndrome
clues: Bloody diarrhea followed by pallor, decreased urine output, and petechiae

complications.name: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
clues: Dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, decreased skin turgor

complications.name: Pyelonephritis
clues: Flank pain, fever, costovertebral angle tenderness
Urinalysis with white blood cells and bacteria

special_populations.differences: Higher risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli; may present with irritability, poor feeding, and bloody diarrhea.
Higher risk of severe dehydration, bloodstream infection, and death; may have milder symptoms but more rapid progression.
Urinary tract infection can ascend to pyelonephritis and trigger preterm labor; antibiotics must be chosen carefully.
Higher risk of invasive disease and sepsis; may have less prominent gastrointestinal symptoms.

key_questions.question: When did the diarrhea start, and how many times a day are you going?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset 1-3 days after exposure; frequent stools; duration under 10 days

key_questions.question: Is there blood or mucus in the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Bloody diarrhea suggests Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome

key_questions.question: Did the vomiting start before or after the diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting after diarrhea; vomiting first suggests viral gastroenteritis

key_questions.question: What have you eaten in the last few days, especially ground beef, unpasteurized milk or juice, or raw produce?
key_questions.looking_for: Undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized dairy or juice, unwashed vegetables or sprouts

key_questions.question: Have you had contact with farm animals, petting zoos, or someone with diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Animal contact or a sick contact with similar illness

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently, especially to an area with poor sanitation?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent travel consistent with travelers' diarrhea

key_questions.question: Do you have burning with urination, going more often, or urgency?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysuria, frequency, urgency suggesting urinary tract infection

key_questions.question: Do you have pain in your back or side, fever, or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Flank pain with fever and chills suggests pyelonephritis

key_questions.question: How much are you drinking, and how much urine are you making?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor intake or decreased urine output suggests dehydration or kidney injury

key_questions.question: Have you taken antibiotics recently, or been in the hospital?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics or hospitalization for resistant or healthcare-associated strains

key_questions.question: Do you take immunosuppressants, steroids, or proton pump inhibitors?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression or acid suppression raising risk of invasive disease

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, kidney disease, or a weakened immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that raise the risk of severe or invasive infection

key_questions.question: Do you use a urinary catheter or have you had urinary procedures?
key_questions.looking_for: Catheter or instrumentation as a source of urinary infection

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes antibiotic choice and raises risk of ascending infection

key_questions.question: Any new sexual partner or recent sexual activity?
key_questions.looking_for: Sexual activity as a risk factor for urinary tract infection

key_questions.question: Any rash, bruising, or unusual bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Petechiae or bruising suggesting thrombocytopenia from hemolytic uremic syndrome

key_questions.question: Any confusion, lightheadedness, or fainting?
key_questions.looking_for: Altered mental status or hypotension suggesting sepsis or severe dehydration

reasoning_points: Acute diarrheal illness or urinary symptoms with a compatible exposure history
Watery diarrhea that may become bloody, with crampy abdominal pain and low-grade fever
Dysuria, frequency, urgency, or flank pain suggesting urinary tract infection
Risk factors such as undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized products, animal contact, female anatomy, or catheter use
Leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance and possible dehydration on labs
Urinalysis with leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and white blood cells in urinary infection
Stool culture or Shiga toxin testing identifies the organism in diarrheal illness
Urine culture confirms E. coli urinary tract infection
Blood cultures positive in invasive or bloodstream infection
Complications such as hemolytic uremic syndrome, dehydration, pyelonephritis, or sepsis considered

easy: Young child with bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked ground beef
Classic watery then bloody diarrhea with severe cramps
Urinalysis with positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase in a woman with dysuria
medium: Older adult with mild diarrhea and dehydration but no fever
Pregnant woman with urinary symptoms and risk of ascending infection
Patient with recent antibiotic use and resistant organism
Diarrhea with no clear food exposure
hard: Infant with irritability, poor feeding, and bloody diarrhea progressing to hemolytic uremic syndrome
Immunocompromised patient with sepsis and minimal gastrointestinal symptoms
Older adult with confusion and hypotension from E. coli bloodstream infection
Bloody diarrhea followed by pallor, decreased urine output, and thrombocytopenia
